title: U.S. House · California's 11th Congressional District
area: The city and county of San Francisco.

context.text: This is an open seat. Incumbent Nancy Pelosi, first elected in 1987, did not run for re-election. Because California uses a top-two primary, two Democrats — San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and state Senator Scott Wiener — advanced to the general election; Wiener received 40.7% and Chan 29.7% of the vote in the 12-candidate primary. Saikat Chakrabarti, who came in third with 17.9%, endorsed Chan, as did Pelosi and U.S. Senator Adam Schiff. Wiener was endorsed by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, San Francisco Board of Supervisors President Rafael Mandelman, and the California Democratic Party. As of July 14, 2026, the Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, and Sabato's Crystal Ball all rated the general election as solidly or safely Democratic.

candidates.name: Connie Chan
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary with about 29.7% of the vote.
candidates.currentRole: Member, San Francisco Board of Supervisors, District 1 (since 2021)

summary.text: Connie Chan is a member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, representing District 1 since her election in 2020, and chairs the Board's Budget Committee. Born in Hong Kong and raised in San Francisco, she worked as a community organizer and in city government, including as a legislative aide and as a staffer for then-District Attorney Kamala Harris, before running for office. She is running for the open 11th District seat on a platform that her campaign describes as a working people's plan, with an emphasis on affordability and community input on development.

background.text: According to her campaign website, she was born in Hong Kong and moved to San Francisco at age 13 with her mother and younger brother; the family obtained a rent-controlled apartment in Chinatown.
Earned a high school diploma from Galileo High School and a bachelor's degree from the University of California, Davis.

Began her career as a volunteer Chinese interpreter with the San Francisco Bar Association's Volunteer Legal Outreach and as a community organizer for SF SAFE and the Community Youth Center, according to her campaign website.

In 2006 she became a legislative aide to then-Supervisor Sophie Maxwell. She later worked as a public safety and communications aide and Asian American and Pacific Islander community liaison for then-District Attorney Kamala Harris, as a legislative aide to then-Supervisor Aaron Peskin, and as a representative of then-Assemblymember Kevin Mullin.

Held administrative roles at the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department and at City College of San Francisco; in her 2020 Ballotpedia survey she describes about fifteen years in leadership positions at those two institutions, including overseeing capital projects and the implementation of Free City College.

First elected to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, representing District 1 (the Richmond District and surrounding neighborhoods), in 2020; Ballotpedia lists her tenure as beginning in 2021 and her term as ending in 2029.

Chair of the Board of Supervisors Budget Committee since February 2023, and a member of the San Francisco County Transportation Authority, the Local Agency Formation Commission, and the Free City College Oversight Committee, according to her campaign website. She says she created a $400 million revenue risk reserve in the 2025-2026 city budget.

Advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary, where she received 29.7% of the vote, to the general election for the seat Nancy Pelosi is leaving. Per her campaign website, she lives in the Richmond District with her partner, a San Francisco firefighter, and their son.

priorities.text: In her Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey response, said she would work to create affordable housing, lower the cost of health care, education, and child care, and take on large corporations that drive up prices.
priorities.quote: I know how families are struggling to pay for every day costs. I'll work to create housing our working families can afford, push to lower the cost of health care, education and child care and take on the big corporations that drive up prices.

priorities.text: Campaign site's "Working People's Plan" says she will fight to empower working families, support strong communities and economic opportunity, reform the tax and budget system, and restore what she calls fundamental democratic rights.
On housing policy, has emphasized community input and protecting residents from the unintended consequences of rapid change, according to Axios San Francisco.

positions.summary: Her campaign site says she will commit resources for housing and to protect tenants, and her survey answers call for strengthening tenant protections, including fully funded free legal counsel.
Her campaign site says she supports Medicare for All and will work to enact it.
positions.quote: Connie Chan supports Medicare for All which guarantees that every American has a right to health care

positions.summary: Her campaign site says she will fight for access to the full range of reproductive health care, including abortion.
positions.quote: Connie will always fight for access to the full range of reproductive health care including abortion and affordable contraception.

positions.summary: In her Candidate Connection survey she says she will fight tariffs that she says are driving up costs for working families.
positions.quote: I'll fight Trump and tariffs that are driving up costs for working families

positions.summary: Her campaign site says she supports a Green New Deal investing in clean energy to move away from fossil fuels.
positions.quote: Connie supports a Green New Deal to invest in clean energy that reduces greenhouse gases, moves us away from fossil fuels and foreign oil, and creates good paying jobs.

positions.summary: In her Candidate Connection survey she says she will fight to end the Trump administration's immigration policies and get ICE out, while working for pathways to citizenship.
positions.quote: I'll fight to end those policies and get ICE out

positions.summary: Her campaign site says she will work with organized labor to raise the national minimum wage.
positions.quote: raise the national minimum wage and secure fair wages for all workers

positions.summary: Her campaign site says she will be an immediate sponsor of the Block the Bombs Act, which would bar transfers of weapons used by the Israeli military in Gaza.
positions.quote: Connie Chan will be an immediate sponsor of the Block the Bombs Act which would prohibit the United States from transferring weapons that have been used by the Israeli military in Gaza.

record.text: Elected to represent District 1 on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 2020 and re-elected since.

candidates.name: Scott Wiener
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary with about 40.7% of the vote.

summary.text: Scott Wiener is a California state senator representing San Francisco since 2016 and a former member of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. An attorney by training, he is known for authoring housing-streamlining legislation and has chaired the Senate Budget and Housing committees. He is running for the open 11th District seat on his legislative record, which his campaign describes as including more than 100 state laws.

background.text: According to his official and campaign biographies, he grew up in New Jersey, the son of a small business owner and a public school teacher, and attended public schools.
Holds a bachelor's degree from Duke University and a law degree from Harvard Law School, and spent a year in Chile on a Fulbright Scholarship doing historical research.

Spent fifteen years practicing law before holding elected office: as a law clerk for Justice Alan Handler of the New Jersey Supreme Court, in private practice at Heller Ehrman White & McAuliffe, and as a Deputy City Attorney in the San Francisco City Attorney's Office.

Has lived in San Francisco's Castro neighborhood since 1997. Before office he co-chaired the Alice B. Toklas LGBTQ Democratic Club, BALIF, and the San Francisco LGBTQ Community Center, and served on the national board of the Human Rights Campaign, according to his Senate biography.

Represented District 8 on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors from 2011 to 2016; his office says he authored laws there on paid parental leave, water recycling and solar power in new developments, and expediting affordable housing approval.

First elected to the California State Senate (District 11, succeeding Mark Leno) in 2016. His district includes San Francisco, Broadmoor, Colma, and Daly City and portions of South San Francisco and San Bruno.

In the Senate he chairs the Elections Committee and previously chaired the Budget, Housing, and Human Services committees; he also sits on the Public Safety, Judiciary, Transportation, and Privacy committees.

His office lists among his authored measures SB 35 and SB 423 (housing permit streamlining), SB 79 (housing near transit), SB 822 (net neutrality), SB 253 (corporate emissions disclosure), and SB 855 (mental health and addiction coverage).
Advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary, where he received 40.7% of the vote, to the general election for the seat Nancy Pelosi is leaving.

priorities.text: Campaign site says he is a nationally recognized leader on housing, citing California streamlining laws he authored that led to construction of tens of thousands of homes, including 3,000-plus below-market-rate units in San Francisco.

Says he will push for Medicare for All and, in the meantime, work on health care affordability by capping insulin at $35 per month, reducing prior authorizations, and lowering prescription drug prices.
Says he will fight to protect immigrant communities, citing his authorship of first-in-the-nation legislation making it illegal for ICE agents to wear masks.

positions.summary: Campaign site says he authored California's most consequential housing-streamlining laws and helped build the statewide YIMBY movement, and will push federal policy to lower housing costs and build more homes.
Says he will fight to protect reproductive freedom in California and nationally, citing his work fortifying state protections for providers and patients after the overturning of Roe v. Wade.
Supports Medicare for All and says he will work to reverse federal cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act.
Says he will fight for an assault weapons ban, safe storage requirements, and funding to keep communities safe from gun violence.
Says he will fight to protect immigrant communities and "abolish ICE," citing legislation he authored to end ICE agents' use of masks and to allow lawsuits against ICE for rights violations.
Says he passed a first-in-the-nation law requiring large corporations to disclose carbon emissions and will take on corporate polluters in Congress.

record.text: Elected to the California State Senate, District 11, in 2016; authored more than 100 state laws, according to his campaign, including housing-streamlining and LGBTQ-protection legislation.
Represented District 8 on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors from 2011 to 2016.
